claim: Pro-social behavior comprises actions that improve the well-being of others.
source: Pro-social behavior comprises actions that improve the well-being of others (Eisenberg et al., 1989)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Eisenberg et al., 1989, which provides scholarly support for this definition.

claim: Pro-social behavior is found widely in the animal world.
source: Pro-social behavior comprises actions that improve the well-being of others (Eisenberg et al., 1989) and is found widely in the animal world (Owens and Owens, 1984; Wilkinson, 1984; Lee, 1987; Heinrich and Marzluff, 1995; Warneken and Tomasello, 2006; Nowbahari et al., 2009; Yamamoto et al., 2012; Baden et al., 2013; Clay and de Waal, 2013; Hatchwell et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to studies documenting pro-social behavior across various animal species.

claim: Pro-sociality within a group promotes individual survival and reproduction.
source: Pro-sociality within a group promotes individual survival and reproduction (Hamilton, 1984; Preston and de Waal, 2002; Decety and Svetlova, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hamilton, 1984; Preston and de Waal, 2002; and Decety and Svetlova, 2012.

claim: In humans, pro-social behavior is modulated by the degree of affiliation and is extended preferentially towards in-group members.
source: In humans, pro-social behavior is modulated by the degree of affiliation and is extended preferentially towards in-group members and less often toward unaffiliated others (Hornstein, 1978; Cialdini et al., 1997; Preston and de Waal, 2002; Levine et al., 2005; Sturmer et al., 2006; Lamm et al., 2010; Echols and Correll, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations documenting in-group bias in human pro-social behavior.

claim: Humans can and often do act pro-socially towards strangers.
source: Yet humans can and often do act pro-socially towards strangers (Batson et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Batson et al., 2005.

claim: Rodents manifest emotional contagion.
source: Rodents manifest emotional contagion (Langford et al., 2006; Chen et al., 2009; Jeon et al., 2010; Knapska et al., 2010; Panksepp and Lahvis, 2011; Akyazi and Eraslan, 2014; Atsak et al., 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to studies demonstrating emotional contagion in rodents.

claim: Rodents manifest cooperation.
source: Rodents manifest emotional contagion (Langford et al., 2006; Chen et al., 2009; Jeon et al., 2010; Knapska et al., 2010; Panksepp and Lahvis, 2011; Akyazi and Eraslan, 2014; Atsak et al., 2011), cooperation (Rutte and Taborsky, 2007; Viana et al., 2010; Tsoory et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rutte and Taborsky, 2007; Viana et al., 2010; and Tsoory et al., 2012.

claim: Rodents manifest helping behavior.
source: Rodents manifest emotional contagion (Langford et al., 2006; Chen et al., 2009; Jeon et al., 2010; Knapska et al., 2010; Panksepp and Lahvis, 2011; Akyazi and Eraslan, 2014; Atsak et al., 2011), cooperation (Rutte and Taborsky, 2007; Viana et al., 2010; Tsoory et al., 2012), and helping (Ben-Ami Bartal et al., 2011; Church, 1959; Rice and Gainer, 1962).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ben-Ami Bartal et al., 2011; Church, 1959; and Rice and Gainer, 1962.

claim: Sprague-Dawley rats learn to release SD cagemates trapped in a restrainer.
source: We previously found that Sprague-Dawley (SD) rats learn to release SD cagemates trapped in a restrainer (Ben-Ami Bartal et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work (Ben-Ami Bartal et al., 2011).

claim: Rats helped trapped strangers by releasing them from a restrainer, just as they did cagemates.
source: We found that rats helped trapped strangers by releasing them from a restrainer, just as they did cagemates.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Rats did not help strangers of a different strain, unless previously housed with the trapped rat.
source: However, rats did not help strangers of a different strain, unless previously housed with the trapped rat.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Pair-housing with one rat of a different strain prompted rats to help strangers of that strain.
source: Moreover, pair-housing with one rat of a different strain prompted rats to help strangers of that strain, evidence that rats expand pro-social motivation from one individual to phenotypically similar others.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Fostered rats helped strangers of the fostering strain but not rats of their own strain.
source: As adults, fostered rats helped strangers of the fostering strain but not rats of their own strain.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data from the fostering experiments.

claim: Strain familiarity, even to one's own strain, is required for the expression of pro-social behavior.
source: Thus, strain familiarity, even to one's own strain, is required for the expression of pro-social behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the fostering experiment data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Most rats in both SD cagemate (75%) and SD stranger (83%) conditions acted pro-socially, learning to release the trapped rat.
source: Most rats in both SD cagemate (6/8, 75%) and SD stranger (10/12, 83%) conditions acted pro-socially, learning to release the trapped rat, and becoming openers (Figure 1; see Methods for opener definition).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing the proportion of rats that became openers in each condition, with reference to Figure 1.

claim: Rats in the SD cagemate and SD stranger conditions were similarly active as measured by velocity.
source: Rats in the two conditions were similarly active as measured by velocity (two-tailed Student's t test, p>0.05)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test) of velocity measurements.

claim: Rats in the SD cagemate and SD stranger conditions spent similar amount of time near the trapped rat.
source: spent similar amount of time near the trapped rat (two-tailed Student's t test, p>0.05)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test) of proximity measurements.

claim: Rats in the SD cagemate and SD stranger conditions began to open the door on around the same day.
source: and began to open the door on around the same day (4.0 ± 1.1 days for trapped cagemates; 3.7 ± 0.8 for trapped strangers, mean ± SEM).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data comparing the day of first opening between conditions.

claim: Rats were as motivated to help strangers as they were to help cagemates.
source: Thus, rats were as motivated to help strangers as they were to help cagemates, showing that individual familiarity is not required for pro-social behavior in rats.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the similar helping behavior observed in both cagemate and stranger conditions.

claim: Individual familiarity is not required for pro-social behavior in rats.
source: Thus, rats were as motivated to help strangers as they were to help cagemates, showing that individual familiarity is not required for pro-social behavior in rats.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the finding that rats helped strangers as readily as cagemates.

claim: SD rats did not release LE strangers with only a minority (25%) becoming openers.
source: SD rats did not release LE strangers with only a minority becoming openers (4/16, 25% openers; Figure 2; Video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing the proportion of openers in the LE stranger condition, with reference to Figure 2 and Video 1.

claim: Most SD rats in the LE cagemate condition became openers (71%).
source: In contrast, most SD rats in the LE cagemate condition became openers (5/7, 71%; χ2, p=0.04)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis (chi-square test) showing a significant difference.

claim: SD rats in the LE cagemate condition learned to open the restrainer on average on day 3.8.
source: learning to open the restrainer on average on day 3.8 ± 1.7 (mean ± SEM, Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data with reference to Figure 2.

claim: Rats help strangers of their own strain but not strangers of a different strain.
source: Thus, rats help strangers of their own strain but not strangers of a different strain, suggestive of an in-strain bias for pro-social behavior.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the differential helping behavior observed between same-strain and different-strain strangers.

claim: Short-term, paired-housing with a rat from a different strain is sufficient to motivate helping for that individual rat.
source: Moreover, short-term, paired-housing with a rat from a different strain is sufficient to motivate helping for that individual rat.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the LE cagemate condition data showing that SD rats helped LE cagemates.

claim: Most SD rats familiar with one LE individual became openers for LE strangers (67%).
source: In contrast to SD rats with no exposure to the LE strain, most SD rats familiar with one LE individual became openers for LE strangers (8/12, 67%; χ2, p=0.03).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis (chi-square test) showing a significant difference.

claim: SD rats familiar with one LE individual learned to open the door on average on day 4.0 for LE strangers.
source: They learned to open the door on average on day 4.0 ± 1.0 despite a lack of individual familiarity with the trapped LE rat (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data with reference to Figure 2.

claim: Social experience with one individual rat of a different strain is sufficient to motivate helping towards unfamiliar members of that strain.
source: This experiment shows that social experience with one individual rat of a different strain is sufficient to motivate helping towards unfamiliar members of that strain.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the LE familiar condition data showing that prior exposure to one LE rat led to helping of LE strangers.

claim: Only 1 of 8 fostered SD rats (12.5%) became an opener for trapped SD strangers.
source: Fostered SD rats did not help trapped SD strangers (Figure 4; Video 2). Only 1 of 8 fostered SD rats (12.5%) became an opener
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the fostering experiment, with reference to Figure 4 and Video 2.

claim: Rats are not innately motivated to help their own strain.
source: establishing that rats are not innately motivated to help their own strain.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the fostered+SD condition data showing that fostered rats did not help their own strain.

claim: Fostered rats helped LE strangers (62.5%).
source: In contrast, fostered rats did help LE strangers (5/8, 62.5%; χ2, p=0.04)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis (chi-square test) showing a significant difference.

claim: Fostered rats were more anxious than naturally reared rats.
source: Fostered rats were noticeably more anxious than naturally reared rats.
evidence: This is an observational claim supported by subsequent behavioral data.

claim: Fostered rats spent more time in the corners of the arena than naturally reared rats in open-field testing.
source: In open-field testing conducted prior to the experiment, fostered rats spent more time in the corners of the arena than rats in other conditions (33.1 ± 2.7 s/min for fostered rats; 25.0 ± 1.9 s/min for naturally reared rats; files with open field data for SD cagemate and SD strangers were corrupted and therefore not included; two-tailed Student's t test, p<0.02; Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data with statistical analysis (t-test) and reference to Figure 5A.

claim: Fostered rats that opened the restrainer began to do so significantly later than naturally reared rats.
source: Moreover, fostered rats that opened the restrainer began to do so significantly later (day 8.0 ± 1.1 for fostered rats; 4.5 ± 0.5 for all other rats; two-tailed Student's t test, p<0.01; Figures 1–2, 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data with statistical analysis (t-test) and reference to multiple figures.

claim: Most rats in familiar strain conditions became openers (74%) whereas only 21% of rats in unfamiliar strain conditions did.
source: Most rats in familiar strain conditions became openers (33/47, 74%) whereas only 21% (5/24) of rats in unfamiliar strain conditions did (χ2, p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by aggregated experimental data with statistical analysis (chi-square test) showing a highly significant difference.

claim: Rats tested with a familiar strain experienced opening the restrainer door as rewarding.
source: Rats tested with a familiar strain experienced opening the restrainer door as rewarding, as they typically opened it on consecutive days (Figure 6B–C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the pattern of repeated opening behavior, with reference to Figure 6B-C.

claim: Rats tested with unfamiliar strains rarely opened on consecutive days.
source: In contrast, rats tested with unfamiliar strains rarely opened on consecutive days, suggesting that opening was not rewarding for these animals.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pattern of non-repeated opening behavior.

claim: Open field performance and alarm calls were not different for familiar and unfamiliar strain conditions.
source: As open field performance and alarm calls were not different for familiar and unfamiliar strain conditions (Figure 5C), it is unlikely that trait anxiety or the trapped rat's distress accounts for the results.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing no significant differences, with reference to Figure 5C.

claim: Rats tested with a trapped cagemate were significantly more active prior to door-opening than rats tested with a stranger.
source: Rats tested with a trapped cagemate were significantly more active prior to door-opening than rats tested with a stranger (MMA, p<0.05, Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (MMA) of activity data, with reference to Figure 7A.

claim: There was no difference in the distance from the restrainer between rats tested with cagemates and strangers.
source: However, there was no difference in the distance from the restrainer in these conditions (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing no significant difference, with reference to Figure 7B.

claim: Rats were equally motivated to help, but not equally aroused by, a trapped cagemate and stranger.
source: These results demonstrate that rats were equally motivated to help, but not equally aroused by, a trapped cagemate and stranger.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the differential activity levels despite similar helping behavior.

claim: Openers spent more time around the closed restrainer than did non-openers.
source: Prior to door-opening, openers spent more time around the closed restrainer than did non-openers (two-tailed Student's t test, p<0.01; Figure 8A; Video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test) of proximity data, with reference to Figure 8A and Video 1.

claim: Significantly less fights were observed for openers than for non-openers following the trapped rat's exit from the restrainer.
source: Following the trapped rat's exit from the restrainer, significantly less fights were observed for openers than for non-openers (two-tailed Student's t test, p<0.01; Figure 8A).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test) of fighting behavior data, with reference to Figure 8A.

claim: For openers, baseline anxiety was positively correlated with the first day of opening.
source: Only for openers, baseline anxiety was positively correlated with the first day of opening (Figure 8B)
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis with reference to Figure 8B.

claim: Anxiety negatively impacts successful helping in the presence of pro-social motivation.
source: suggesting that anxiety negatively impacts successful helping in the presence of pro-social motivation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation between anxiety and delayed opening in openers.

claim: Rats were less active before door-opening compared to after door-opening.
source: Rats were less active before door-opening compared to after door-opening (repeated measures ANOVA, main effect, p<0.001; Figure 8C).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (repeated measures ANOVA) of activity data, with reference to Figure 8C.

claim: Non-openers showed significantly reduced activity prior to door opening, which was not the case for openers.
source: Pairwise comparisons found that this effect was due to significantly reduced activity in non-openers prior to door opening, which was not the case for openers (pairwise comparisons, p<0.05; Figure 8C).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (pairwise comparisons) with reference to Figure 8C.

claim: Helping another rat is flexibly applied to select others based on previous social experience.
source: This study demonstrates that helping another rat, by releasing it from a restrainer, is flexibly applied to select others based on previous social experience.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from all experimental findings in the study.

claim: It is the prior social experience of the free rat with any member of the trapped rat's strain that determines the target group for helping.
source: Rather, it is the prior social experience of the free rat with any member of the trapped rat's strain that determines the target group for helping.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the pattern of helping behavior across all experimental conditions.

claim: Rats help another rat from a given strain (same or different) only if they have previously lived with a member of that strain.
source: Thus, rats help another rat from a given strain (same or different) only if they have previously lived with a member of that strain.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from all experimental findings in the study.

claim: Rats pick up sensory cues from their cagemates that are retained and utilized to discriminate between strangers.
source: Rats pick up sensory cues from their cagemates that are retained and utilized to discriminate between strangers that share those cues and those that do not.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed pattern of helping behavior toward familiar versus unfamiliar strains.

claim: Strain identity is meaningless without social experience during development.
source: The present study effectively demonstrates that strain identity is meaningless without social experience during development.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the fostering experiment results.

claim: Fostered rats raised without social interactions with their own strain were not motivated to help strangers of their strain.
source: Fostered rats raised without social interactions with their own strain were not motivated to help strangers of their strain, compelling evidence against an innate bias for pro-social behavior towards one's own kind.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the fostering experiment data.

claim: Neither kinship nor perceived similarity is needed to motivate pro-social behavior in primates.
source: This finding is congruent with studies showing that neither kinship nor perceived similarity is needed to motivate pro-social behavior in primates (Batson et al., 2005; Horner et al., 2011; Baden et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies in primates.

claim: Relying on social experience rather than genetic similarity for guiding pro-social behavior allows animals to flexibly adapt to different circumstances.
source: Yet, relying on social experience rather than genetic similarity for guiding pro-social behavior has an added value in that it allows animals to flexibly adapt to different circumstances (Dugatkin, 2002).
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation to Dugatkin, 2002.

claim: Door-opening does not depend on reward from either motor mastery or social contact.
source: We have previously excluded the possibilities that door-opening depends on reward from either motor mastery or social contact (Ben-Ami Bartal et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: It is unlikely that rats were motivated to open the restrainer by aggressive or anti-social motivations.
source: In addition it is unlikely that rats were motivated to open the restrainer by aggressive or anti-social motivations (Myer and White, 1965) because conflict between the free and trapped rats was minimal for opener pairs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed low levels of conflict in opener pairs, with a citation to Myer and White, 1965.

claim: Rats open the restrainer door in order to terminate the trapped rat's distress.
source: Given the greater interest in the trapped rat shown by openers and the lack of aggressive interactions between opener pairs, the authors favor the interpretation that rats open the restrainer door in order to terminate the trapped rat's distress.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation based on the observed behavioral patterns.

claim: Helping behavior has been demonstrated toward strangers in other animals, including humans.
source: This result is consistent with previous demonstrations of helping behavior expressed toward strangers in other animals, including humans (Warneken and Tomasello, 2006; Batson et al., 2007; Loggia et al., 2008; Custance and Mayer, 2012; Tan and Hare, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to studies in various species.

claim: Emotional contagion has been demonstrated for both individually familiar and unfamiliar mouse pairs.
source: While emotional contagion has been demonstrated for both individually familiar and unfamiliar mouse pairs (Chen et al., 2009; Jeon et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2009 and Jeon et al., 2010.

claim: Emotional contagion may be facilitated by individual familiarity.
source: it may be facilitated by individual familiarity (Langford et al., 2006; Jeon et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Langford et al., 2006 and Jeon et al., 2010.

claim: Work in dogs and primates supports a familiarity effect for emotional contagion.
source: Work in dogs and primates further supports a familiarity effect for emotional contagion (Palagi et al., 2009; Campbell and de Waal, 2011; Silva et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies in dogs and primates.

claim: Empathy is the capacity to share and recognize the emotional states of another.
source: Empathy, the capacity to share and recognize the emotional states of another (Decety, 2011)
evidence: The claim is a definition supported by a citation to Decety, 2011.

claim: Empathy often motivates approach and pro-social behavior and caring in humans.
source: Empathy, the capacity to share and recognize the emotional states of another (Decety, 2011), often motivates approach and pro-social behavior and caring in humans (Eisenberg and Miller, 1987).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Eisenberg and Miller, 1987.

claim: The empathic response involves activation of common neural networks for processing one's own and another's distress.
source: The empathic response involves activation of common neural networks for processing one's own and another's distress (Decety et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Decety et al., 2012.

claim: Some forms of empathy are primarily dependent on subcortical neural structures that are phylogenetically conserved across mammalian species.
source: Some forms of empathy are primarily dependent on subcortical neural structures that are phylogenetically conserved across mammalian species (Decety and Svetlova, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Decety and Svetlova, 2012.

claim: Emotional contagion is a fundamental component of empathy resulting when the emotion of one individual evokes a matching emotional state in another individual.
source: Emotional contagion, a fundamental component of empathy resulting when the emotion of one individual evokes a matching emotional state in another individual (Preston and de Waal, 2002)
evidence: The claim is a definition supported by a citation to Preston and de Waal, 2002.

claim: A rodent form of empathy is the main motivation for the helping behavior observed in the study.
source: We would argue that a rodent form of empathy, as defined above, is the main motivation for the helping behavior observed in our studies.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of their findings.

claim: The absence of door-opening for rats of unfamiliar strains likely reflects a reduced empathic arousal of the free rats in these conditions.
source: Moreover, the absence of door-opening for rats of unfamiliar strains likely reflects a reduced empathic arousal of the free rats in these conditions.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of their findings.

claim: The selectivity with which rats engage in helping behavior is evidence that releasing a trapped rat is an intentional social behavior.
source: The selectivity with which rats engage in helping behavior is further evidence that releasing a trapped rat is an intentional social behavior, congruent with an empathic drive to help some rats, but not others.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed selective helping behavior.

claim: Through social interactions, rats form affective bonds that elicit empathy and motivate helping.
source: We conclude that through social interactions, rats form affective bonds that elicit empathy and motivate helping.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the overall pattern of experimental findings.

claim: Rats form groups based on social experience.
source: This motivation to help is extended to strangers of familiar strains, showing that rats form groups based on social experience.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the finding that rats help strangers of familiar strains.

claim: Rats base the bias for pro-social behavior on group membership, as is the case for humans.
source: As is the case for humans (Xu et al., 2009; Mathur et al., 2010), rats base the bias for pro-social behavior on group membership.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study findings, with citations to human studies for comparison.

claim: For humans, a diverse social experience is effective in mitigating pro-social bias.
source: And as for humans, a diverse social experience was effective in mitigating such bias (Chiao et al., 2008; Elfenbein and Ambady, 2003; Madsen et al., 2007; Telzer et al., 2013; Zuo and Han, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to human studies.

claim: For rats, genetic similarity does not influence pro-social motivation.
source: Moreover, we have demonstrated that for rats, genetic similarity does not influence pro-social motivation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the fostering experiment results.

claim: Groups are socially defined in rats.
source: Rather, groups are socially defined.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the overall pattern of experimental findings.

claim: Social bias is hard to overcome through cognitive effort in humans.
source: Whereas social bias is hard to overcome through cognitive effort (Dovidio et al., 2002; Johnson et al., 2002; Amodio et al., 2004; Correll et al., 2007)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to human studies.

claim: There exists at least one mechanism for altering group membership that does not require complex cognition.
source: our results support the existence of at least one mechanism for altering group membership that does not require complex cognition.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study findings showing that simple social experience can alter helping behavior.

claim: The door to the restrainer could only be opened from the outside and thus only by the free rat.
source: The door to the restrainer could only be opened from the outside and thus only by the free rat.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental apparatus design.

claim: If a free rat failed to open the door within 40 min, the experimenter opened it halfway.
source: If a free rat failed to open the door within 40 min, the experimenter opened it halfway, allowing the trapped rat to exit the restrainer.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental protocol.

claim: All rats were males and all free rats were from the SD strain.
source: All rats were males and all free rats were from the SD strain.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental subjects.

claim: Sessions were repeated for 12 days.
source: Sessions were repeated for 12 days.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental protocol.

claim: Cagemates were pair-housed for 2 weeks prior to the experiment.
source: Cagemates were pair-housed for 2 weeks prior to the experiment.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental protocol.

claim: On each day of testing in the SD stranger condition, a different stranger was trapped in the restrainer.
source: On each day of testing, a different stranger, to whom the free rat had no prior exposure, was trapped in the restrainer.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental protocol for the SD stranger condition.

claim: Rats that opened the restrainer on two sequential days, and did so at least three times were termed 'openers'.
source: Rats that opened the restrainer on two sequential days, and did so at least three times were termed 'openers'.
evidence: This is a definition of the operational criterion used in the study.

claim: Two SD pups were placed into each LE litter on either P0 or P1 in the fostering experiments.
source: Two SD pups were placed into each LE litter on either P0 or P1 (average 0.3 ± 0.1).
evidence: This is a description of the fostering protocol.

claim: When the SD pups were on average 6.4 days old, one SD pup was removed, leaving a single male SD pup in the LE litter.
source: When the SD pups were on average 6.4 ± 0.2 days old, one SD pup was removed, leaving a single male SD pup in the LE litter.
evidence: This is a description of the fostering protocol.

claim: Most SD male pups (14/16) were exposed to one SD littermate for no more than 7 days in the fostering experiments.
source: Thus, most SD male pups (14/16) were exposed to one SD littermate for no more than 7 days (days when the pups' eyes were closed).
evidence: This is a description of the fostering protocol and exposure conditions.

claim: The pup with the maximal exposure to at least one SD pup (11 days) was transferred when his eyes were open and became the sole opener in the fostered+SD condition.
source: The pup with the maximal exposure to at least one SD pup (11 days) was transferred when his eyes were open; this rat became the sole opener in the fostered+SD condition.
evidence: This is a description of a specific case in the fostering experiment and its outcome.

claim: The nursing behaviors of dams were not different between rats in fostered+LE and fostered+SD conditions.
source: The proportions of each behavior recorded were not different between rats in fostered+LE and fostered+SD conditions (1-way repeated measures ANOVAs, p>0.11).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (repeated measures ANOVA) of maternal behavior.
